title: The decree determines the act but leaves the faculty flexible: true in the divided, not the composite sense
source_text: XII. Ad id vero quod objicitur, posito decreto divino circa aliquem actum humanae voluntatis, voluntatem humanam non posse aliter agere, adeoque tolli ejus in agendo indifferentiam, in qua posita est libertas, respondent, non quidem simul consistere ut Deus decreverit voluntatem aliquid agere, istud vero voluntas non agat, aut aliter agat: sed tamen decretum Dei non obstare quominus in voluntate maneat potestas aliter agendi: quoniam decretum Dei actum quidem determinat, sed facultatem relinquit flexibilem ad oppositum. Ac proinde quum homo juxta Dei decretum aliquid agit, vere dici potest illum posse non agere, & aliter agere, quia, videlicet, Deus decrevit quidem ut hoc agat, sed tamen ita agat ut potens maneat aliter agendi: Adeoque, licet in sensu composito verum non sit, posito decreto Divino voluntatem posse agere, vel non agere, verum est tamen in sensu diviso: quia cum decreto Divino non consistit quidem actus oppositus, sed optime tamen consistit facultas ad actum oppositum.
pass_a_gloss: XII. But to that which is objected, that, a divine decree concerning some act of the human will being posited, the human will cannot act otherwise, and so its indifference in acting, in which freedom is placed, is taken away, they answer, that indeed these do not stand together, that God has decreed the will to do something, but the will does not do it, or does otherwise: but yet the decree of God does not hinder that there remains in the will a power of acting otherwise: since the decree of God indeed determines the act, but leaves the faculty flexible to the opposite. And therefore when a man does something according to the decree of God, it can truly be said that he can not do it, and do otherwise, because, namely, God decreed indeed that he do this, but yet that he so do it that he remains able to act otherwise: And so, although in the composite sense it is not true, the divine decree being posited, that the will can act, or not act, yet it is true in the divided sense: because with the divine decree the opposite act indeed does not stand, but yet the faculty for the opposite act stands perfectly well.
pass_b_english: It is objected that once God has decreed some act of the human will, the will cannot act otherwise, so its indifference in acting, where freedom lies, is removed. They answer that it cannot both be true that God decreed the will should do something and that the will does not do it or does something else.

Yet God's decree does not prevent the will from keeping the power to act otherwise. The decree determines the act, but leaves the faculty able to turn to the opposite. So when a man does something in keeping with God's decree, it can truly be said that he is able not to do it and to act otherwise. God decreed that he should do this, but should do it in such a way that he remains able to act otherwise.

Thus, granted the divine decree, it is not true in the composite sense that the will can act or not act; but it is true in the divided sense. The opposite act cannot stand together with the divine decree, but the faculty for the opposite act stands with it perfectly well.
